claim_text: Continuous delivery and continuous deployment are empirically distinguishable practices, and organisations may remain able to release frequently without fully automating production deployment.
Fault injection and resilience-testing studies operationalise reliability by exposing faults, measuring degradation or testing resilience properties under controlled scenarios.
Incident automation is commonly applied to detection context, characterisation, aggregation, profiling and triage before or alongside recovery.
Automated root-cause analysis and query recommendation are represented as investigation or decision-support mechanisms rather than evidence of autonomous recovery.
A charted prototype study reports dependency-aware self-healing across application and cloud-service failure scenarios in its evaluated context.
Direct practice evidence concerns incident response, expert debugging, post-incident learning and controlled deployment under reliability constraints.
The accessible corpus contains no controlled participant comparison of reliability-automation conditions with validated workload, trust, understanding or decision-quality measures.
Technical studies use heterogeneous metrics and event boundaries, so detection, recovery initiation, recovery completion and impact should be recorded as separate events before comparison.
Industrial studies depend on proprietary data or configurations while prototypes expose different levels of code, scenario and environment detail.
The accessible evidence is rich in adjacent cloud-native and online-service operations but contains limited controlled evidence centred on continuous-delivery recovery decisions.
permitted_use: Scope rationale; bounded by database-access limitation.
